# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has evolved dramatically since the introduction of balloon angioplasty, with drug-eluting stents (DES) becoming the contemporary standard of care [1]. Despite their efficacy, permanent metallic stents are associated with persistent limitations including chronic vessel caging, impaired vasomotion, neoatherosclerosis, and very late stent thrombosis [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery, followed by complete resorption, theoretically restoring vascular physiology and eliminating the long-term liabilities of permanent implants [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, clinical evidence, and current status of BVS technology in PCI.

## Rationale and Device Characteristics

The concept of a fully resorbable scaffold addresses the notion that mechanical support is required only transiently during the vessel healing process [4,5]. The most extensively studied device, the Absorb everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold (Abbott Vascular), consisted of a poly-L-lactide backbone with a poly-D,L-lactide coating eluting everolimus, designed to resorb over approximately three years [6]. Potential advantages include restoration of vasomotor function, late luminal enlargement, plaque regression, and preservation of future surgical and percutaneous treatment options [7,8]. Other devices investigated include the magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold and various polymeric alternatives [9].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The ABSORB cohort A and B studies provided first-in-human data demonstrating feasibility, with imaging confirming scaffold resorption and restoration of vasomotion at long-term follow-up [6,10]. These promising findings led to larger randomized trials. The ABSORB II trial compared the Absorb scaffold with the Xience metallic everolimus-eluting stent, initially showing comparable short-term outcomes [11]. However, three-year results revealed that the scaffold failed to meet its co-primary endpoints, with greater late lumen loss and a higher rate of device thrombosis [12].

## Pivotal Randomized Trials and Meta-Analyses

The ABSORB III trial, the largest pivotal study, randomized over 2000 patients and demonstrated non-inferiority for target lesion failure at one year [13]. Nonetheless, longer-term follow-up showed an increased rate of target lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis between one and three years [14]. Similar signals emerged from ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China [15,16]. The AIDA trial, an all-comers study, was halted early after reporting markedly increased rates of definite or probable scaffold thrombosis compared with metallic stents [17].

Multiple meta-analyses synthesized these data, consistently demonstrating an excess risk of scaffold thrombosis, particularly very late thrombosis occurring after one year, alongside higher rates of myocardial infarction [18,19,20]. The increased thrombotic risk was attributed to greater strut thickness, malapposition, scaffold discontinuities during resorption, and uncovered struts [21,22].

## Mechanistic Insights and Implantation Technique

Intravascular imaging studies elucidated mechanisms of failure, highlighting the importance of optimal implantation technique [22,23]. The thicker struts (approximately 150 µm) of first-generation BVS predisposed to flow disturbance and delayed healing [21]. The "PSP" technique—adequate lesion preparation, appropriate sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—was shown to improve outcomes and reduce adverse events [24,25]. Avoidance of small vessels and careful patient selection were similarly emphasized [26].

## Regulatory and Market Developments

In light of accumulating safety concerns, the Absorb scaffold was withdrawn from commercial sale in 2017 [27]. Regulatory authorities issued warnings regarding its use, particularly in small vessels [27]. Despite this setback, interest in the bioresorbable concept persisted, with continued investigation of thinner-strut next-generation devices and magnesium-based scaffolds, which demonstrated favorable preliminary signals in selected studies [9,28].

## Future Directions

The first-generation BVS experience provided crucial lessons regarding device design and procedural technique [29]. Newer scaffolds with reduced strut thickness, improved radial strength, and faster resorption kinetics are under development and early clinical evaluation [28,30]. Whether these iterations can realize the theoretical benefits of bioresorption while overcoming the thrombotic liabilities of their predecessors remains to be determined through rigorous long-term randomized trials [29,30].

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represented a conceptually attractive paradigm shift in PCI, aiming to provide transient support without the long-term consequences of permanent metallic implants [4]. However, first-generation devices were associated with increased rates of scaffold thrombosis and target lesion failure, leading to withdrawal of the leading device [17,27]. The field continues to evolve, and refined next-generation scaffolds combined with optimized implantation strategies may yet fulfill the original promise of this technology [29,30].
